To combine two object pronouns in the right order: indirect before direct (me lo, te la, nos los).

23 December, evening, at Ecaterina’s flat in Bucharest. Marta has come to spend her first Christmas without her grandfather in Bucharest. Andrei is home for the holidays. Ecaterina has finished the book.
Marta, here’s the manuscript. I’m giving it to you before anyone else.
To me? You haven’t sent it to Inés yet?
No. I’ll send it to her once you’ve read it. If there’s anything you don’t like, tell me.
I’ve already read the whole thing. She lent it to me yesterday and I couldn’t sleep.
You read it in one night?
Not in one night: in one night and a breakfast. I even forgot to eat.
Andrei likes every book with a lorry in it.
Give it to me. I’ll take it to bed and give it back to you tomorrow.
There’s no need to give it back. Keep it. It’s a copy for you.
Then I won’t read it: I’ll drink it in.

When you attach pronouns, the stress stays on the verb’s syllable: DÁ-me-lo, DÁ-se-lo, DÁN-do-se-lo. That’s why the written accent is used.
“se lo” is pronounced together with the verb, without a pause: [se-lo-DI], [se-lo-man-DA-re]. Pronouns are never stressed.
Four syllables, stress on the first: QUÉ-da-te-lo. Don’t move the stress onto “te”.
When there is both an indirect object (to whom?) and a direct object (what?), the INDIRECT comes first:
“Le lo” and “les la” don’t exist: «Le lo di» ✗ → «Se lo di» ✓. “Se” can mean “to him”, “to her”, “to you (formal)” or “to them”; if it isn’t clear, add “a él / a ella / a usted / a ellos”.
Se lo voy a dar. / Voy a dárselo.
Se lo estoy dando. / Estoy dándoselo.
When you attach two pronouns, you almost always add a written accent to keep the verb’s stress: dar → dárselo, dando → dándoselo, da → dámelo.
To Marta I gave the manuscript.
The manuscript she finished on 20 December.
That photo was taken by Faustino.
Spanish repeats the indirect object with “le”, and a direct object placed at the start of the sentence is picked up again with “lo / la”. Without the pronoun, the sentence sounds unfinished.

Ecaterina finished the book on 20 December, at ten past five in the morning. She wrote the last sentence, read it quietly, moved it twice and put it back where it had been. Then she switched off the computer, made herself some tea and stood watching through the window as snow began to fall on the rooftops of Bucharest. She didn’t call anyone. She said later that she had wanted to keep that moment to herself for a few hours, the way you keep a present before giving it to someone.

At nine she printed two copies at the copy shop on the corner. The young man serving, a student with blue hair, asked her whether it was a thesis. Ecaterina told him no, it was a novel. He asked her what it was about. Ecaterina answered: a bookshop, a letter and forty years. The young man thought for a moment and said he would buy it when it came out. Ecaterina thanked him and left him a tip, which he refused to accept.

Andrei arrived in Bucharest on the evening of the 21st, with his new coat and a suitcase full of presents. Begoña had given him ten days’ holiday and told him that if he came back with a single good photo of Romania, she would let him off. His mother was waiting at the airport with a scarf she had knitted all through November. She put it round his neck before she even kissed him. His father took his suitcase and asked whether he had bought the coat in the sales. Andrei said yes. His father nodded, satisfied.

That same night, his father offered to show him the bridges of Bucharest in the snow, so he would have something to send Begoña. They went out at eleven, with two flasks of tea and the camera. Señor Dan introduced them one by one, like old friends: this one he had repaired in 1998, that one had a problem with its supports that nobody wanted to see, the one over there was the most beautiful in the city and the worst maintained. Andrei took forty photos. His father appeared in thirty-two of them, although he didn’t notice.

The next day, Ecaterina asked him to come over. She gave him one of the two copies of the manuscript, wrapped in brown paper. She told him she wanted someone young to read it before anyone else, someone who hadn’t known that Madrid. Andrei took it home at six in the evening. At seven in the morning he was still reading in the kitchen, wearing his scarf, his coffee gone cold. He read the whole thing in one go. He forgot to have dinner. His mother found him like that when she woke up and didn’t dare say anything.

Marta arrived on the 23rd. It was her first Christmas without her grandfather, and Pilar was going to spend it with her husband’s family in Cádiz. When Ana heard that Marta was going to be alone in the flat on the calle del Prado, she called her and wouldn’t let her say no. Marta landed at Otopeni with a small suitcase and a woolly hat she had bought at Madrid airport, because she had left her own at El Mostrador. As she stepped off the plane, the Bucharest cold took her breath away.

Ana took her straight from the airport to the centre, because she wanted to show her Bucharest before it got dark. She showed her the Athenaeum, Lipscani Street with its Christmas lights and the door of the Instituto Cervantes, where she worked and where Costel and Señor Dan had taken the exam. Marta photographed everything on her phone, her fingers frozen. At a street stall she bought some hand-knitted woollen gloves. The woman who sold them asked her where she was from. When Marta said “Madrid”, the woman gave her a scarf as well.

That same evening, Ecaterina gave her the other copy. She gave it to her in her living room, in front of Andrei, with a sentence Marta would never forget: “I’m giving it to you before anyone else.” Ecaterina explained that she hadn’t sent it to Inés yet, that she would send it once Marta had read it. Marta took the manuscript to bed. She didn’t read it: as she said later, she drank it in. At four in the morning, Ana, who was sleeping in the next room, heard someone crying very quietly, and didn’t go to see who it was, because she already knew.

On the morning of the 24th, Marta came down to breakfast with swollen eyes and the manuscript under her arm. She gave it back to Ecaterina, although Ecaterina had told her to keep it. She said she had only one correction. On page 212, where Ecaterina described the night she left Madrid, she had written that Andrés never knew why she had gone. Marta told her that wasn’t true. That her grandfather had always known. That he had told her many times, when she was a child, without ever saying the name: “She left because they needed her more than I did.”

Ecaterina sat very still. She asked Marta to repeat the sentence. Marta repeated it, slowly, in Spanish. Ecaterina picked up a pen, crossed out the sentence on page 212 and wrote above it, in shaky handwriting, the one Marta had told her. Then she closed the manuscript, took off her glasses and sat for a long time without speaking. Andrei, who had seen it all from the doorway, took out his camera. But he didn’t take the photo. Begoña had taught him that some photos are better not taken.

Later, alone in the kitchen, Ecaterina asked Marta something she hadn’t dared to ask for months: whether her grandfather had ever reproached her for leaving without saying goodbye. Marta shook her head. She said never. That her grandfather only ever reproached himself for one thing: never having asked for her address in Bucharest. For years he had thought that if he had asked for it, he could have sent her that letter. Ecaterina laughed through her tears. She told her she had reproached herself for forty years for exactly the opposite.

At midday, Ecaterina called Pilar in Cádiz. She read her the new sentence on page 212, the one Marta had given her. At the other end of the line there was a long silence, and then a sound that could have been the Cádiz wind or could have been something else. Pilar told her she had heard her father say that sentence only once, the night he closed the bookshop in 1994, and had never understood who he was talking about. She asked her to keep the first copy of the book for her. Ecaterina said she had already promised it to someone else, but would keep her the second.

They spent Christmas Eve at Ana and Mihai’s house, the house that had belonged to Rosa Elena’s great-grandmother, the one master Ilie had renovated. Carmen and Juan had also come from Madrid; it was their first Christmas in Romania and they wouldn’t take their coats off even indoors. Rosa Elena had decorated the Christmas tree on her own, with more baubles at the bottom than at the top, because she couldn’t reach the top. At the very tip, instead of a star, she had hung a cardboard lorry.

Elena, Mihai’s mother, arrived too, with a sugar-free cozonac she had been perfecting for years since she was diagnosed with diabetes, and so did Grandpa Gheorghe, whom Mihai had driven to fetch from the village that morning, along a road covered in snow. Grandpa was ninety-six and walked into the house as if it were his own, which in a way it was. When he saw Marta, he greeted her as “the Spanish girl from August” and asked whether she had brought the bottle. Marta had brought it, empty again. Grandpa said that apparently in Madrid they were still drinking very fast.

At six, Lola’s parcel arrived. Faustino had taken it to the post office in person, and it contained turrón for everyone, a new La Lámpara bookmark for Ecaterina and Marta’s hat, the one she had left in the café. Rosa Elena ate the whole chocolate turrón before anyone could stop her, and then told everyone about it very proudly. Costel, who had had his eye on it too, said it didn’t matter, he preferred the almond one. Nobody believed him.

Grandpa Gheorghe and Juan, who didn’t have a single word in common, sat together on the sofa with a bottle of țuică and understood each other perfectly for two hours. Juan taught him to say “olé”; Grandpa taught him to say “noroc”. They drank a toast every ten minutes, alternating the two words, and laughed harder each time. Carmen warned Juan from the kitchen that țuică wasn’t wine. Juan replied that he knew, that was why he liked it so much. Grandpa, understanding nothing, said “olé”.

Mrs Florica and Carmen had divided the kitchen between them like two generals: the left half for the sarmale, the right half for the Segovia-style roast lamb. At seven there was a small disaster: Carmen burnt the first batch of croquetas, and Mrs Florica dropped a whole tray of cozonac on the floor. The two of them looked at each other. They burst out laughing at the same time. Mihai said it was the closest thing to world peace he had ever seen.

After dinner the carol singers arrived: four children from the neighbourhood, each with a woolly hat and a paper star on a stick. They sang three carols at the door, with a lot of cold and more enthusiasm than tunefulness. Marta didn’t understand the words, but was moved all the same. Rosa Elena translated them for her one by one, making half of it up. When the children finished, Juan, who never said anything, took out his wallet and gave them twenty euros. Mrs Florica explained that a few walnuts and a piece of cozonac were enough. Juan said that in Madrid carols were more expensive.

When the children had left, Marta said that in Spain they had carols too, and that they couldn’t go to bed without one. She sang “Los peces en el río”, first alone and very embarrassed, then with Carmen and Juan, who knew it by heart, and finally with Rosa Elena, who didn’t know the words but made up some about a lorry drinking from the river. Grandpa Gheorghe kept time by tapping his stick on the floor. Mrs Florica said the Spanish sang as if they were at a wedding.

At eleven they opened the presents. Andrei gave Ecaterina Faustino’s 1985 photo, printed large and framed: her laughing with her head thrown back, Andrés beside her, the green sign behind them. Ecaterina looked at it for a long time without saying anything. Then she said she didn’t remember ever being so young. Marta gave Ecaterina an envelope. Inside were her grandfather’s reading glasses, the tortoiseshell-framed ones he wore in the bookshop. “I’ve brought them so you can correct the book’s proofs,” she said. “He would have wanted you to wear them.”

Ecaterina had a present for Marta too. It was the first page of the manuscript, the original one, written in July at three in the morning, with the sentence about the suitcase, the dictionary and the certainty of leaving soon. She had signed it and written underneath: “For Marta, the first reader. You asked me for it, so now it’s your turn to carry it.” Marta put it in the inside pocket of her coat, next to her heart, and said she wasn’t going to show that page to anyone, not even Inés.

Costel had no presents for anyone, or so he said at first. But when everyone had finished, he took a crumpled envelope out of his pocket and gave it to Ana. It was a copy of his registration confirmation for next year’s DELE C1 exam. He had signed up the week before, without even knowing his B2 mark yet. Ana asked him whether he was mad. Costel said yes, a little, but he had learnt from Ecaterina that you shouldn’t wait forty years for anything. Señor Dan, from the sofa, said quietly that he was thinking about it too.

Señor Dan’s wife, sitting next to him, laughed and said her husband wasn’t thinking about it at all. He had signed up too, the day before, in secret, and she knew because she had seen the confirmation email on his phone. Señor Dan went bright red. Costel hugged him so hard his glasses went crooked and told him that, in that case, the Thursdays in the cab would go on. Ana said she would have to buy another stopwatch, because the two of them had already broken the first one.

Around midnight it began to snow properly. Rosa Elena had fallen asleep on the sofa, hugging her toy lorry, with traces of turrón on her face. Carmen and Juan watched the snow through the window as if it were a fireworks display, because in Madrid they hardly ever saw it. Andrei went out into the garden with his camera and photographed the house lit up, with the snow falling and the windows glowing. Later he would send that photo to Begoña. She would reply with two words: “Not bad.”

When Andrei came back in, Rosa Elena had woken up. She was sitting on the sofa, half asleep, watching the snow through the window. She asked Marta whether Señor Andrés could see the snow too. Marta took a moment to answer. Then she told her yes, he was surely seeing it from Lola’s lamp, which was like a window. Rosa Elena thought about this very seriously, nodded, pulled the blanket over herself and went back to sleep. Marta sat beside her for a while, without moving, so as not to wake her.

Ecaterina went home at one, with Andrei and Marta, through the white, empty streets. In the living room, she switched on the computer. She opened the manuscript, found page 212 and corrected the sentence in the file, just as she had corrected it by hand that morning. Then she wrote the dedication, which she had left until last: “For A., who left the light on. And for everyone who has brought me to it.” Marta, reading over her shoulder, squeezed her arm without saying anything.

It was a quarter to two in the morning on 25 December when Ecaterina sent the manuscript to Inés Vidal. In the email she wrote just three lines: “Dear Inés: here it is. I’m sending you the whole thing, with a last-minute correction Marta gave me. Merry Christmas.” She pressed the send button and stared at the screen until the confirmation message appeared. Then she told Marta that she hadn’t sent a letter in forty years, and that at last she had forgotten to be afraid.
